to the interiors where you have dry farming or barr en area, you find farmers sell because 
they do not have holding capacity. The moment they harvest others have to sell because 
they have no method of keeping it because warehousi ng, godowns, and so on are yet to 
come in a big way. Therefore, my request is this. Good weather code should be implemented 
from end-to-end, from the soil to the market. The t hird point is that there is a very good 
opportunity this year to launch, what I call, bridging the yield gap movement. If you look at 
all the scientific data, in almost all our crops there is a very big gap. Normally, you say China  
  is producing so much and India is producing so mu ch. But I am not talking about irrigated 
crop, even other crops, rain-fed crops, whether it is jowar, whether it is bajra, whether it is 
pulses or whether it is oilseeds, almost 50 per cent more, 50 to 100 per cent more, is the yield 
•gap. The bridging the yield gap movement is an exceedingly important one, and this year we 
should try our very best. Now that several crores o f farmers will be relieved from the debt 
trap, it is all the more important that we enable t hem. In other words, relieving the debt is 
only one step in the process. The more important st ep is how to get them one feet in terms 
of agriculture. Very many areas, today, I have earlier also said in the House, like Jharkhand, 
where there are enormous areas which are single crop land. There is 1400 mm of rainfall, as 
the hon. Member said, and there is a National Rain- fed Area Authority now. These all 
should be geared up now, how do you make a single crop land into a double crop land. Part 
of the naxalite problem will also stop because an idle mind is a devil's workshop. There are a 
large number of people who are idle in these areas.  The next point, today, and I think for 
the foreseeable future our food security system, pa rticularly, the PDS, which is going to 
depend very heavily on Punjab and Haryana and Western U.P. We call this the heartland of 
the Green Revolution. They are the only sheet ancho rs of our PDS System. This year also 
because they are producing more and giving more. No w, this area is in deep distress. The 
water table is going down. In fact, the very districts which are the most important agriculturally 
Amritsar, Jalandhar, Ludhiana, Patiala. In all these areas, the water table has gone very deep 
and it is still going very deep. This is why in thi s area Conservation Farming should be 
launched, in a big way, during coming South-West Mo nsoon period. If you look at the US 
Farm Bill, the largest amount of money goes to conservation farming because if farm ecology 
and farm economics go wrong, nothing else will go r ight in agriculture. And, therefore, I 
plead with the Agriculture Minister, with thehelp of the Punjab Government and the Haryana 
Government, to launch a groundwater recharge moveme nt this year; a large movement for 
recharging their groundwater. There are many methods, I would not take time now. But this 
is exceedingly important because if this region, st arts deteriorating and farmers out of 
frustration sell their land for other purposes, non-agricultural purposes, we will become  
 ever dependent oh import for our food security. Th erefore, it is in national interest to 
safeguard this particular heartland and nurture it. My next point, Sir, is this whole question 
of mismatch between production and post harvest technology. It is enormous. Several hon. 
Members have already mentioned about the post harve st losses in our country. Even 
today, the paddy is dried on the road. Road and roof are the most important areas for drying. 
I think it is important that we launch a large post -harvest technology, the lab to land 
programme, which will take all modern methods. Now recently in Kuttanad in Kerala, very 
good rice crop was damaged because there was not en ough method of harvesting, storing 
and drying. So, I think, we can ill afford to make our farmers face 21 st century agriculture 
with practically no support in service at all. No support services, our infrastructure, the post 
harvest infrastructure is very poor. I again reques t that we must make a large lab-to-land 
programme in post harvest technology.

Lastly, Sir, a question was raised by Shri Amar Singhji about genetically modified crops and 
also he mentioned about the National Commission recommendation. Genetic modification is one 
process of what we call the evolution of genetics. What is important is no technology is good or 
bad. It is the same as with atomic energy, you can make a bomb and you can also make energy. A 
knife can kill a person or cut a fruit. The technology itself is neither good nor bad. What is important 
is the use of the technology, it must be in our country, pro-small farmer technology, pro-nature, 
pro-poor and pro-woman technology. Take one example, BT cotton is one of the factors in the 
farmers' suicides in Vidharbha; high cost, I would say not merely BT cotton, but high cost 
agriculture. There are now excellent varieties with the ICAR, same BT genes in varieties. The 
advantage with the variety is that the farmers can keep their own seeds. They don't have to go to 
the company every year. For a hybrid, a farmer has to go to the company. Our Plant Variety 
Protection and Farmers' Rights Act assures the power to the farmers to keep their own seeds 
and therefore, I would again request the President of the ICAR that ICAR should concentrate on 
pro-small farmer biotechnology and also take on areas like salinity tolerance, drought tolerance, 
flood tolerance and also pests and diseases and so on. Also, finally, a task force, which I chaired 
and which presented our report four years ago to the hon. Agriculture Minister, recommended a 
very credible National Bio-Technology Regulatory Authority, which will weigh the risks and 
benefits in a very transparent manner so that it has a high political, professional, public and media 
credibility. I think, it is high time we have some structures. Otherwise, there is a lot of confusion, 
people have to go to court every time, get some sto ps, some suggestions are made and 
therefore, my plea would be that you don't throw aw ay the baby with the bath water. 
Technologies can be made use of, technologies can be abused but what we need is a method by 
which abuse can be prevented. I am happy that Shri Shanta Kumarji referred to the Sixth Five Year 
Plan and also the allocations made. That was the only Plan where the agricultural growth rate was 
higher than the economic growth rate. I say it with some pride because I was involved in that 
process in the Sixth Five Year Plan is developing the agricultural strategy. But, let me summarise 
in one word: In farming, we say, you reap as you sow. You could have put enough resources, at 
that time nearly five million hectares of additional area, under irrigation every year; that was the 
provision. If you look at the Sixth Five Year Plan, twelve per cent of the total Budget went to 
irrigation alone. Therefore, I think, it is important in this country; those of us who are here are 
discussing the fate of 70 per cent of our people, the largest chunk of our people and also the other 
30 per who depend upon them for their food, this is a very, very serious situation and global 
situation is serious. National situation could be s erious because we are also — fortunately 
thanks to enlightened policies — increasing consumption in the country. For example, NREGA 
will increase consumption for those who are poor. But, then, our food security must be based on 
homegrown food, not imported food. We may import occasionally but agriculture is the mainstay 
of the livelihood security of the majority of our population.

single year, in the last five years. Leave alone 4 per cent, we have not achieved 3 per cent or 
2 per cent. With regard to foodgrains our growth ha s, now, reduced to 0.92 per cent. When 
the globalised economy was started, we had, in this  House, discussed about the food 
safety. At that point of time, the foodgrain growth was 1.9 per cent, whereas the increase in 
population was 2.1 per cent. Now, from 1.9 per cent  per annum increase, it has reduced to 
0.92 per cent. That is the seriousness of the probl em. Whenever a need arises, there would 
be no foodgrains in the granaries. Hon. Member, Shr i Shanta Kumar, told that at that point 
of time there were 64 million tonnes of foodgrains in the FCI godowns. Now, even the 
minimum bufferstock is not there in the FCI godowns . So, the situation is very alarming. 
But, unfortunately, the Government is not at all serious in the matter. Here, the most important 
thing is the need for investment. What is the reaso n for this failure? The reason for the 
failure is the lack of public investment in agriculture. That is the main reason for this failure. 
During the last 10-15 years, the public investment in agriculture has declined very sharply. 
Now, it is just 5.9 per cent of GDP. And, there lies the weakness. So, because of this, there is 
a sharp fall in the production and productivity. Un less you are able to improve the 
productivity and production, how can you solve this problem? The other day, we discussed 
about the price rise. The prices of foodgrains are increasing; the prices of pulses are 
increasing; the prices of edible oils are increasin g. The, average price of one kilogram dal 
whether it is green peas, whether it is sambar dal, whether it is moong dal, whatever dal it  
" is—is Rs. 50/- The average income of an agricultu re worker is less than Rs. 50/- per day So, 
he would get only one kilogram dal for his one day's income. That is the kind of situation in 
the country. But the Government is sleeping over the issue. It is all because of your policies. 
This is because of the adverse impact of the cut in  the subsidy in the food production. The 
input cost is increasing day-by-day. Fifteen years ago, the per acre input cost of cotton was  
. Rs. 2500. Now, it is Rs. 13,000/-. So, there is 500 per cent increase in the input cost. There is 
a wide gap between the input cost and the price of a product. There is a wide gap between 
the input cost and the income of the farmers. So, f or the poor farmers, the agriculture 
became a loss-making enterprise. Seventy per cent o f the farmers are poor. So, every year 
they have been getting into the debt trap. Now, after 10-15 year, they are forced to sell their 
land. That is the most serious crisis in the agricultural sector. Have you ever tried to address 
this problem? Every year, 3.5 million farmers are s elling their land and becoming landless. 
That is the creation of the on-going agrarian policy in our country. The Central Government 
is not at all serious about this problem of the far mers. He is selling his livelihood; he is 
selling whatever little land he has. He is migratin g to the cities and becoming an industrial 
labour. In such a situation, what relief are you giving to these people? Unfortunately, the  

Discussion on the working  [28 APRIL, 2008]     of the Ministry'of Agriculture 243  
Government is not at all serious about the problem. And, because of the lack of investment, our 
productivity is hit like anything. We are not able to address the problem of acute price rise. If I 
come and meet the hon. Minister of Agriculture with  regard to problems of farmers, or, the 
productivity, or, lack of foodgrains, there will be  no proper answer. That is the difficulty. Sir, 
there was a failure in production. Last year itself , that is, during 2007-08, the   target for 
production of wheat was 75.5 million tonnes, but th e achievement was 74.81 million tonnes. In 
case of cereals, it was 37.50 million tonnes and th e production achieved was 36.09 million 
tonnes only. So, this is the situation. The target was there, but we were not ' able to achieve this 
production. The country's average production growth  rate was 3.62 during the period 1984-85 
to 1995-96. Now, in 2004-05, it has been reduced to 0.92 per cent. This is the situation.  
Then, Sir, we have to think about the debt problem faced by the poor farmer. Here also,  
now the Government has announced a good programme for waiver of the agricultural loan. I 
would like to congratulate the Government for this programme, But, Sir, will this relief 
actually go to the poor farmer? This is the questio n. We are all aware that around half of the 
farmers are taking loans from moneylenders. Waiver of institutional loans means, only the 
rich farmer will get benefit of this programme. Now, you have announcd the programme. You 
have kept a ceiling of 2 1/2 hectares for farmers. In Vidharbha, a farmer with 7 or 8 or 10 
hectares of land is called a poor farmer. He will n ot get the benefit. Vidharbha is a place 
where we are facing acute problem. But the farmer, in that particular locality, will not get the 
benefit. The farmer in Western Maharashtra will get the benefit. The rich farmer will get the 
benefit, but the poor farmer will not get the benef it. How do you solve this problem? Some 
concrete steps are to be taken to solve this proble m. In Kerala, we have set up a separate 
Commission called the Agricultural Debt Relief Comm ission. This particular Commission 
has been appointed and it will go through the detai ls of different kinds of loans, whether 
institutional loans or non-institutional loans, whe ther loans taken from moneylenders or 
from some other sources. This particular Commission  will go through the details of the 
loans taken by the farmers and will give an advice. On the basis of that advice, the Government 
will be in a position to help the poor and debt-rid den farmer. Under this Scheme, only those 
farmers who take loans from the nationalised banks or cooperative banks will get relief. My 
humble request is that the Government should come f orward with a concrete proposal. It 
should not use the traditional methods. I do not kn ow how you are going to implement it,  
My humble request is that the advice of organisatio ns like the Agriculture Debt Relief 
Commission, formed by the Government, should also b e taken note of. Their 
recommendations should be considered for providing debt relief to the farmers. Since in 
Kerala we have a specific Commission. I request you  to coordinate with that Commission 
for this Debt Relief Programme.  
Sir, farmers are in a debt trap. This point should also be taken note of. In Karnataka, 
around 64 per cent of the farmers are in crisis. In Kerala, 62 percent of the farmers are facing 
this loan problem. In Andhra Pradesh, 84 per cent of the farmers are facing this loan problem. 
This is the condition. So, a viable programme shoul d be started to help a large number of 
farmers who are living in distressed condition in these areas.  
Then, Sir, there is an issue of subsidies. Here also, Sir, the difficulty is there because in 
the present situation, our farmers have to compete with the rich and corporate farmers living 
in the Western countries. This point should also be  taken note of How are you going to 
formulate your policy on agriculture without considering this aspect? O.ur farmers have to  

244   Discussion on the working   [RAJYASABHA]  of the Ministry of Agriculture  
compete with the farmers who are getting higher subsidies in the Western countries. For 
example, the U.S. gives a subsidy of $ 4.7 billion to its cotton growers' having a crop value 
of $ 3.9 billion. That is the situation. Their subsidy is more than the input. So, naturally, they 
are in a position to compete. They are in an advantageous position in the world market in 
the field of agriculture. Sir, in the Western countries, the multinational companies are getting 
a subsidy of three dollars per cow per day. That is the thing. Sir, this is the situation. The 
dream of a poor Indian farmer is to get a re-birth in US as a cow so that we would get double 
wage. This is the situation. ...(Interruptions)...  
So, there is highly subsidised farming from outside., and here whatever investment is 
coming, it is coming only from the poor farmers. The poor farmer has to bear the expenditure. 
So, through you, Sir, I request the Government to seriously think of the situation and come 
Out with some concrete proposals in Order to help the poor farmers in our country.  
Similarly, Sir, we announce many programmes in our Budgets but unfortunately, we do 
.not implement them properly. We are not able to do that. Just see, Sir, how many Committee 
are there which we have appointed so far. The National Commission on Farmers, the National 
Development Council's Sub-Committee on Agriculture, the Eleventh Plan Working Groups, 
Rangarajan Committee on Financial Inclusion and Radhakrishnan Committee on Agriculture 
Indebtedness are among them. There are half a dozen committees. Only committees are 
there, but there are no concerte proposals.  
Similarly, Sir, when we come to Budget proposals and their implementation, the situation 
is no different. The National Food Security Mission have a moderate plan to increase the 
production of rice by 10 million tonnes, wheat by 10 million tonnes and pulses by 2 million 
tonnes in the Eleventh Five Year Plan. But, Sir, what is the allotment? Sir, there is no proper 
allotment; only objective is there. Then, Sir, kindly go through the allotment. You go through 
the situation. The Budget allocations in most of the sectors do not match with the proposals. 
...(Time-bell)... Sir, I will take just two-three minutes more. In the case of crop science, 
during 2007-08, the actual Budget allocation was just Rs. 100 crores against the proposal of 
Rs. 341.05 crores. Similarly, Sir, for the same thing, for 2008-09, against the proposal of 
Rs. 410.93 crores, the allocation is only Rs. 315 crores, i.e., Rs. 96 crores less. For agricultural 
engineering, in 2008-09, the allocation is Rs. 42 crore which is just 36 per cent of the 
proposal of Rs. 115.93 crore. For animal science, against the proposal of Rs. 149.52 crore for 
2007-08, only Rs. 80 crores were sanctioned and for 2008-09, only Rs. 90 crores have been 
allocated against the proposal of Rs. 288.92 crore. For the agricultural extension sector, 
against the proposal of Rs. 538.17 crore, only Rs. 301 crore have been allocated for 2008-09. 
So, you see, Sir, the real allocation is very, very less as compared to the announcements.  
Similarly, Sir, the experience of Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana is also to be taken note of. 
It is a very important programme for the next Five Year Plan. Now, see, Sir, what is the 
experience of the first year of the programme? For this Programme, the Central Government 
has envisaged an outlay of Rs. 25,000 crore for the Eleventh Five Year Plan. That means, on 
an average, per year, Rs. 5000 crore was to be allocated for this Programme. The main 
objective of the Plan is to give incentives to the farmers. Now, that is not at all there. So, Sir, 
the experience of the first year of the Programme is highly disappointing. The outlay was 
only Rs. 1063 crores and the amount released to the States is only Rs. 984.59 crores. So, 
against a target of Rs. 5000, this is the allotment. Sir, just see the approach adopted by the 
Government towards this Programme. A very callous approach has been adopted towards 
this very important Programme. There are only announcements but there is no  

Discussion on the working        [28 APRIL, 2008]     of the Ministry of Agriculture 245  
implementation. There is no allotment from the Budget, and, at the Revised Estimate stage, it 
is further reducing. This is the problem.  
Sir, another area of concern is the milk production . I do not want to go into more details. 
Sir, I would like to say only one thing here. There is an alarming situation. This year, we were 
forced to ban the export of milk powder. There is n o good quality feed available. There 
should be a proper programme for feed and fodder. I t should be linked with the self-help 
groups. That would be more helpful to the milk farm ers. Then, there is this big problem of * 
Avian Flu which occurred recently in West Bengal. S ir, in the recent outbreak of Bird Flu, 
West Bengal alone suffered a loss of Rs. 1500 crore s. It is adversely affecting the poor. 
Government should take proper and effective safegua rds so that such a situation could be ,  
avoided in future.  
Talking of fishermen, they are in acute distress. O ur production of marine products has been 
coming down. There should be an appropriate program me for enhancing it. At present  the 
situation is a very difficult one. You must help them with free ration and other facilities.  
Sir, with regard to Kerala, I have a request to mak e to the hon. Minister. Kerala is a State 
where we have an acute shortage of food grains. It is a State that has the advantage of 
producing cash crops on a large scale. Of course, f or coconut there are some programmes. I 
think whatever announcements have been made with re gard to cocounut plantations should 
be implemented by the Government. With regard to Ku ttanadu special package, I would like 
to say that it would help in increasing the food pr oduction in the State, but the Government 
has to give an assurance that it will be implemente d. Similarly, for a State which has a lower 
production of food grains, a special package must b e announced. Sir, we met the hon. 
Agriculture Minister. He told us that doing that is very difficult as there is no production in our 
State. Our problem is that we produce cash crops. T his earns good foreign currency for the 
country. Since times immemorial, Kerala has had foo d shortage. So, my humble request to 
the hon. Minister is that the Government should ann ounce a special package for increasing 
food grains production in Kerala and grain allotment for Kerala. The Government has to come 
forward with some proposal. The Government must, co nsidering the serious situation and 
the plight of the poor farmers in the country, thin k of a change in the policy. The policy that 
you have been pursuing has not helped in resolving the problems of agricultural workers and 
poor peasants of the country. Also, you must effect ively implement ' the NREGP for 
improving productivity in agriculture. You have to change the present policy and whatever 
policy you are announcing must be implemented.

SHRI GOVINDARAJAR (Tamil Nadu): *Let me thank the c hair for giving me an 
opportunity to speak on behalf of All India Anna Dr avida Munnetra Kazhagam in this 
august House. We are now discussing the performance  of agriculture in general and 
performance of Union Agriculture Ministry in particular.  
We all know that our country is an agricultural country with 70% of the people dependent 
on agriculture as their livelihood.  
That is why Thiruvaluvar the Tamil sage poet emphasized that agriculture is the axis of 
all the industrial activity as every other industry  depend on it and all people go after it in 
Ueneration.  
Our country is one of the foremost countries in agriculture that is carried on in a systematic 
way down the centuries. But if you ask of me whether the Union Agriculture Ministry really 
helps our agriculture sector, my answer would be mo re than 90% of our agriculturists and 
agricultural labourers are being below poverty line. We can not say that they are a better lot 
as they grow food and other basic material through their labour in cultivation. As one 
hailing from an agriculturist's family I would like to draw the attention of this august House 
to the plight of the farmers. Farmers have got this set back because of the wrong policies of 
the Government. The green revolution of the sixty exposed us to Tamil chemical fertilizers 
and insecticides. Cultivable lands have lost there fertile nature due to the increased use of 
artificial manure. The original nature of our culti vable fields have changed because of the 
impact of the chemical fertilizers and insecticides that were introduced by the western world 
after the world wars. In the last four or five decades the use of chemical fertilizers and

insecticides have increased manifold. In 1960-61, a bout five thousand tonnes of fertilizers 
were used by the Indian farmers. To-day we find the  use of such fertilizers have hugely 
increased to 13 lakhs tonnes. The danger of our soil losing its potential is looming large. We 
feel proud that our growth rate has crossed nine percent. But agricultural sector has witnessed 
a growth rate of a mere 2.58%. The rural population  that can not make a living out of 
agriculture have started migrating to the urban areas. Migration of rural poor and agricultural 
labour to urban towns is on the increase. Already u rban areas go through unemployment 
problem. The influx of rural poor to urban areas re sult in their miserable living conditions 
going worse giving rise to health and sanitation problems there.  
Genetically modified and engineered hybrid seeds ha ve also added to the woes of our 
farmers having given rise to the problem our countr y now faces in the agricultural sector. 
This will endanger us further and I would like to d raw the attention of our Minister of 
Agriculture. Particularly imported GM cotton seeds are causing great havoc in the market. 
LRI cotton seeds are rated high for it is cheaper w ith higher yield. But due to globalisation 
and economic liberalization, MNCs especially big US  companies have started supplying 
BT cotton at Rs. 3500/- making huge profit while making our farmers their captive consumers. 
This trend must be arrested.  
According to a report from FAO of UN, about 221 mil lion our people due to abject 
poverty face food scarcity in our country. In order  to overcome the food scarcity there is a 
need to increase food production. But irrigation facilities have not been augmented. Concrete 
measures have not been evolved by this Government. Right from 1996-1997 to 2004-2005 
during those 10 years not much was done to augment irrigation facilities. Annually only 
0.5 percent of lands get water through irrigation. Mega projects have not been conceived 
at all to improve irrigation facilities. Instead the Union Agriculture Ministry point a finger at 
State Governments. There are many bottlenecks for the State Government. Hence the Union 
Government must take up irrigation like Railways an d Posts & Telegraph under its direct 
responsibility.  
It has been stated that more subsidies and grants would be extended to agriculture in the 
Eleventh Five Year Plan. It must be increased to protect the interests of our farming community.  
It has been projected that there will be a sharp fa ll in food production in the next ten to 
twenty years. It would greatly affect our India. The fate of State Governments may even get 
worse. In order to help the farmers, Government mus t ensure that agriculturists get a good 
price for their produce. Now the cost of production  is more than the selling price. This 
affects our farmers. Paddy and Sugarcane must get remunerative price. Essential goods like 
rice, wheat, maize, pulses, cooking oil cost more. Inflation is high. Food production must 
improve and cultivation must be encouraged. In India the cost of agricultural production is 
high. It is higher than even the market price of ag ricultural produce. Food subsidy is Rs. 
31,000 crores. Fertilizer subsidy is Rs. 42,000 crores. But still there is a need to protect our 
farmers.  
When our lecder Dr. Puratchi Thalaivi Amma was the Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu she 
brought about a revolutionary move 'Farmers Protect ion Scheme' to help save the farmers 
and ensure prosperity in their lives. Similar move must be there now. Bio-fuel plantations 
get subsidy and grants and incentives. They must be  provided also to those who cultivate 
and grow food grains. When there is shortage of food grains we must not encourage other

things like cash crops and bio-fuels. This would only result in inflation. This will also result in 
change of Government at the centre.  
Lastly I would like to point out that all the agriculturists have to borrow and remain in debt. 
Almost all the farmers are in debt, they have not made money and do not cemain rich. Our founder 
leader sang that those who drive their car in an arrogant fashion must realize that they can not afford to 
ignore farmers. If the agriculturists decide to leave aside their ploughshares, the world would come 
to a grinding halt. If farmers suffer it would weaken our economy.  
When it comes to debt relief it must be extended to  all the farmers. There must not be any 
segregation as small farmers and marginal fanners. The plight of all the farmers remain the same. This 
must be changed. Our leader Dr. Puratchi Thalaivi Amma has stated that all the * agriculturists must 
get farm loan waivers and the benefit of debt relief measures. This will help all the farmers and the 
farm production. Inflation can be controlled by way of increasing food production. This will help our 
country's economy. Economic growth will lead to self sufficiency and prosperity. We can have 
allround growth with a steady industrial and agricultural growth. We can emerge as a super power then. 
Agriculturists must be encouraged in all possible ways with subsidies, grants, loans at reduced interest 
rates, lesser priced inputs, increased irrigation facilities and remunerative price for their produce 
without being discriminated as small and marginal farmers. Suitable measures in this regard must be 
evolved by the Union Agriculture Ministry. With this I conclude my speech. Thank you.

DR. M. V. MYSURA REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Thank you Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir.  
Sir, 'agriculture in this country is in acute crisi s.' This is not my statement. The hard realities in  
agriculture brought by the Economic Survey of 2007-08 are: Decline in agriculture GDP rate despite 
normal rainfall, decline in rate of growth of foodgrains which are less than  

Discussion on the working  [28 APRIL, 2008]     of the Ministry of Agriculture 259  
population growth, stagnation in foodgrains product ion, decline in agriculture share of 
gross capital formation, decline in agricultural lo ans from 18 per cent as mandated and 
decline in area under foodgrains.  
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI TARIQ ANWAR) in the Chair] 
The Ministry of Agriculture is similar to a farmer's family. Due to paucity of time, I am not 
demanding or asking anything from the hon. Minister. I only wish to highlight whether 
some of the schemes implemented by the Government of India are farmer-friendly. * 
Regarding the Minimum Support Price, the genesis of the M.S.P. is to protect the farmer  
from market price fluctuations. While arriving at the M.S.P, all the costs incurred by farmer 
for producing various crops have to be taken into consideration. This is one of the important 
criteria for arriving at the M.S.P. But, the situation at the grass root level is quite different. It 
is not at all reflecting the actual cost incurred by farmers. I myself, along with press reporters, 
visited Nalgonda district in Andhra Pradesh to asce rtain the factual position at the ground 
level. The Field Assistants, who are mandated to st ay in that village and to obtain the cost 
of cultivation data, are neither staying nor obtain ing the required data from the farmers. 
They are fudging the figures and sending the same to the DES. They are also not obtaining 
the signatures from the farmers. Based on these fudged figures, the Directorate of Economics 
and Statistics is computing the figures. The DES ne ver bothered to compare the data with 
the details obtained by the CACP for the cost of cu ltivation. Due to this, true reflection of 
the cost of cultivation is not arrived.. As a resul t, farmers are suffering and are not getting 
the correct M.S.P So, I am bringing this to the not ice, of the hon..^Minister to review as to 
what is happening at the ground level. It is not on ly happening in Nalgonda district, but it 
is happening throughout the country. The situation is same in the entire country. That is 
why I am requesting the hon. Minister to look into this aspect seriously.  
With regard to Crop Insurance Scheme, I wish to sub mit that the objective of Crop 
Insurance Scheme is to protect the farmers in the event of crop loss due to natural calamities, 
pests and diseases. But, in arriving at the eligibility, I would say that it is not at all helpful to 
the farmer because of impracticable procedures applied by the Department in arriving at the 
crop losses, crop cutting experiments, threshold yields coefficient, etc. Instead of calculating 
the crop loss like this, the Government of India is  taking into consideration the average 
yield of various crops for calculating the MSP. It is also resorting to some other vague * 
procedures. Instead of resorting to this impractica l procedure, the crop losses can be 
estimated by fixing the indemnity by taking into co nsideration the average yield minus 
actual yield. Further, the indemnity criterion, whi ch is followed in other sectors, is not 
followed in the agriculture sector. That's why the Crop Insurance Scheme is not farmer-
friendly. Therefore, I request the hon. Minister to  review the procedure for calculating the 
crop loss by taking into consideration the indemnity criterion.  
So far as the loan waiver scheme is concerned, the limit of two hectares of land is not 
justified. It is not helpful to the farmers who depend on the rain-fed crops. Also, the scheme 
appears to be beneficial to the wilful defaulters, rather than to the honest and regular 
payers, even while they are in distress. As per the  Government of India norms, the kharif 
season starts from 1st April and ends by 30th Decem ber. So, the farmers who had repaid 
their earlier crop loans and had availed of fresh l oans from 01.04.2008 onwards are not 
eligible to get benefit under this scheme. It was b rought to the notice of the hon. Minister 
by other Members also. So, I would like to request the hon. Minister to review the entire 
scheme so that more and more farmers could get bene fit of this scheme.

THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRITARIQ ANWAR): Please conclude.  
SHRI M.V. MYSURA REDDY: I am just concluding, Sir. The ICAR develops agricultural

agricultural growth; it has developed hybrid seeds and other vaieties for various crops; it 
has produced breeder seeds for variety of crops. Bu t, as per the Annual Report, they had 
released 16 hybrid seed rice varieties to the vario us States. But has the Minister ever made 
an assessment as to how many farmers are adopting t he seeds developed by the ICAR, and  
What is the extent of cultivation? I don't think there are many such farmers. I understand that 
majority of farmers are using the seeds developed b y private multinational companies, 
rather than the seeds developed by the ICAR. I thin k, Department's earning through 
sales*, of seeds is Rs. 15 lakhs. It further substa ntiates my argument. Therefore, the seeds 
or hybrid varieties developed by the ICAR are not t he choice of farmer. Such is the 
condition of the ICAR.  
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI TARIQ ANWAR): Please conclude.  
SHRI M.V. MYSURA REDDY: I am concluding within a fraction of minute, Sir. When 
we go through the Annual Report, out of the total b udget of Rs. 1,764 crores. Rs. 1,636

cent. When we have a look at the posts also, the to tal sanctioned posts are 6,428. The 
number of administrative posts is 4,814, and the nu mber of supporting staff is 9,722. So, 
this is the fate of the ICAR. One can very well imagine how the department is functioning. 
The number of scientists is less. The number of sup porting staff as well as the 
administrative staff is more. That's why their research projects are not at all useful to the 
farmers. The farmers are not adopting any technique developed by the ICAR.

SHRI SHARAD ANANTRAO JOSHI (Maharashtra): Thank you, Mr. Vice-Chairman, 
Sir, for giving me this opportunity.  
Sir, at a time when we are debating the working of the Ministry of Agriculture, the 
situation of agriculture in the world as a whole is  becoming threatening and frightening. 
This kind of a situation is repeating itself after 400 years. In the Sixteenth Century, Dr. 
Malthus warned the world for the first time that th e land under cultivation did not 
increase, except in arithmetical progression, and t he population increased in geometrical 
progression, and, therefore, feeding the people wou ld be impossible unless there were 
diseases, wars and large-scale deaths. That problem  was overcome by very innovative 
methods, by improving technology, which has helped us survive today and eat, at least, 
two or three meals a day.  
Sir, the situation that is facing our Minister of A griculture today is much worse than the 
situation that had presented itself at the time of Dr. Malthus. We have a situation where land 
is not only not increasing in arithmetical progress ion, it is actually going down because of 
the Special Economic Zones and because of the vario us Governmental projects. As for 
climate itself, we can see the difference in today' s climate map; practically, the average 
temperature of India is above 40 degrees Centigrade, and even in Vidharbha and some other 
parts of Maharashtra, it has risen above 43-44 degrees Centigrade. I except the temperature 
to touch 46 degrees Centigrade this year and to touch 47 of 48 degrees Centigrade next year. 
And then, there are a number of other problems. New  technology is coming in; Genetic 
Engineering is coming in; Remote Sensing is coming in. And all this is changing the 
dimensions of these problems. Petroleum shortage is  creating another specific problem; 
some of the crops have to be diverted for production of Ethanol or fuel crops. That itself is  

Discussion on the working  [28 APRIL, 2008]     of the Ministry of Agriculture 263  
taking a very large toll on the agricultural situation. With due respect, I would like to warn 
the Minister for Agriculture that this is not a situation which was faced either by Marx or by 
Gandhi and therefore, if you try to find solutions either in Marx or Gandhi, you are going to 
face a tragedy. You will have to think of your own methods, be pragmatic and search for 
India-specific solutions. None of the old dogmas wi ll be able to help you. I would suggest 
some of the things that are required to be done. I have talked in this House quite often about 
the mistakes made in the past. Today, I am in a fri endlier mood and I want to suggest what 
ought to be done hereafter!  
Firstly, recently I read a speech by hon. Shri Sharad Pawar, where the said that it is a pity 
that the farmers have to take the burden of the consumers' requirements. Whenever we talk 
of dearness, whenever we talk of inflation, the burden is invariably shifted to the shoulders 
of the farmers. And this is an aspect which is threatening us right now. Recently, in order to 
curb inflation, we imported oil, which is going to cost dearly the farmer in India in the current 
year and next year, he would be producing less. We are banning the export of non-Basmati, 
rice; we are putting restrictions on the domestic t rading of .the farm produce. All these 
things are going to have their own toll and next ye ar, possibly the farmer may have less 
incentive to produce more than he otherwise had.  
... Sir, I would suggest that the Minister for Agri culture should try to devise a strategy 
where we do riot respect any of the present systems  and permit maximum freedom to the 
farmers as well as to the markets in the best possible manner, so that the problem of striking a 
balance between the consumer and the farmer is sett led by forces of demand and supply ' 
and not the arbitrary interventions of the Government.  
Sir, I would also like to propose to the Minister for Agriculture to create, with immediate 
effect, a Constitutional National Farmers' Commission. It does not exist. There were a number 
of national commissions. I get hundreds of letters every day where farmers are complaining 
about their personal or other difficulties. I wish there were an office that would deal with 
complaints and protestations of this type. And this  should be a Constitutional body and a 
permanent body; the Chairman may change from time to time, but this should be a permanent 
body. The other suggestion that I would like to mak e is in respect of the loan waicver. It is 
a fact that the loan waiver scheme is defective, si mply because it differentiates between 
different borrowers, differentiates between differe nt lenders, differentiates between long 
term and short term loans, and all these differences, which were classical at one time in the 
Marxist literature, have ceased to have any validity today. For example, you cannot say that 
two hectares of irrigated land is the same as two hectares of rain-fed land.  
Similarly, a farmer who takes loan from a bank and borrows from a private moneylender is 
order to repay the loan of the bank at any given time whether he is found to be owing to the 
bank or to the moneylender is a matter of entire chance, and the kind of theatrical remark that 
has been made 'don't pay back the moneylender' will cost you very dearly because he is the 
person who supplies something like 60 to 70 per cen t of the agricultural credit because of 
the special merits he has. Sir, I have found, for example, in Maharashtra itself. (Interruptions)..  
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI TARIQ ANWAR): Please conclude.  
SHRI SHARAD ANANTRAO JOSHI: In various places, for example, even in Kerala, I 
have found a very awkward situation where farmers s hould get the advantage of the loan 
waiver, but for various reasons, they are not able to get it. For exxample, in Kozhikode 
district of Kerala, where the cooperative movement is in the hands of the Communist Party,  

   Discussion on the working   [RAJYASABHA]  of the Ministry of Agriculture  
they enticed the farmers to repay the loan just few days before the 29th February with the 
result that they were not able to get the advantage  of the loan waiver scheme at all. This 
kind of thing has happened in various States and I would request the Minister for Agriculture 
to call a conference of various stakeholders including the farmers' organisations to find out 
what improvements can be made so that the courageou s step that has been taken remain 
the lasting historical achievement.  
The last point that I would. like to make is, it is said not only that the land is decreasing 
but the farmers themselves want to quit agriculture. In this respect what is important, on the 
threshold of the new revolution, is to create and draft a regular exit policy for agriculturist 
that does not necessarily mean only permitting the farmers to quit, but permitting the other 
people, who have the necessary managerial,financial and technical abilities, to come in and 
unless there is a kind of a flush in the agricultur al population, we are unlikely to see the 
population on the farm which can meet the situation that is created together by the climate 
change, by the various technological changes and by 'the fact that water may not be available 
hereafter at all. Thank you.  
SHRI A. A. JINNAH (Tamil Nadu): Respected Vice-Chairman, Sir, today is a red-letter day 
in the annals of my personal life to have the honour of delivering my maiden speech in this 
august House.  
This Rajya Sabha had been adorned by a galaxy of illustrious and eminent personalities. 
Even today, the eminent agricultural scientist, Pro f. M.S. Swaminathan, and other hon. 
Members have given valuable speeches supported by statistics.  
I belong to the minority Muslim community from Tamil Nadu. The protector of minorities. 
Dr Kalaignar Karunanidhi, the Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu and my precious leader of the 
DMK Party offered me a place in this august forum. He used to say that "It is not the halo 
around the hero that is essential but the results of his efforts, the achievements arising out 
of his accomplishments."  
I start my speech with gratitude to three great leaders whose footsteps I follow in all my 
walks of life. At first. I would like to pay my respect to the great rationalist, humanist, social 
reformer and freedom fighter Periyar E.V. Ramaswamy, who opened the eyes of lakhs and 
lakhs of laymen and ladies in the country who suffe red in the darkness of superstition, 
religion and caste. He fought for equality, self-respect, upliftment of the downtrodden and 
social security for women.  
Next I would like to say a few words about the creative genius Arignar Anna, called C.N. 
Annadurai, -LT/ whose knowledge and writings could be compared to Bertrand Russell and 
Bernard Shaw. He created a calibre in public life with his three commandments-Duty, Dignity 
and Discipline.  
Anna was a great democrat and a peace lover. He even respected his political opponents 
and used to say, "the jasmine that grows in the neighbour's garden will also have the same 
fragrance similar to the one in his garden." He adorned this august forum from 1962-1967 
and made matchless speeches.  
Our first Prime Minister of independent India, the light of Asia, Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, 
admired his speech in the Rajya Sabha and praised h im as a worthy Paliamentarian and a 
dignified politician. Anna became the Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu in 1967.

As Lord Tennyson quotes, "The finest things in the world will come and smile at the 
people for a short time and pass to their own end quickly." Anna was the Chief Minister for 
two years in Tamil Nadu before his sudden demise in 1969.  
Then, the incomparable political leader and the man  of the masses. Dr. Kalaignar M. 
Karunanidhi, became the Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu after Anna. He holds the record of 
winning every election that he fought in his politi cal career spanning over 65 years. He 
became the Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu for the fifth time in 2006. He is the statesman who 
stands like a colossus in the political history of Tamil Nadu.  
He is a humble and simple leader who rose to the le vel of conquering the hearts of 
millions of people in Tamil Nadu and the Tamils liv ing all over the world. His loveable 
language and method of expression in public meeting s, the conduction of party system 
created millions of followers and partymen in Tamil  Nadu. He has fought for the state 
autonomy and social justice for the people of our country. He has been my political mentor 
for the past 45 years teaching me the democratic principles and dedication to public life.  
The glorious pages of Tamil Nadu under Kalaignar's regime include flourishing industries, 
development in agriculture and growing numbeer of I.T. parks which are some of the salient 
features of his able and elite administration.  
Kalaignar led the United Progressive Alliance in Tamil Nadu and won all the contested 
40 Lok Sabha seats in the 2004 Lok Sabha elections with the able guidance and leadership 
of the Chairperson of the UPA, Madam Sonia Gandhi. Madam Sonia Gandhi is a charismatic 
and able leader of the Congress Party and the United Progressive Alliance.  
Agriculture is the main occupation of the majority of population in India and it is agriculture 
that sustains the life of the people of our country . In accordance with the Tamil Saint 
Thiruvalluvar's dictum which he said 2500 years ago . "Everything else is secondary to 
agriculture."  
I congratulate the Union Government under the Prime  Ministership of Dr. Manmohan 
Singh, who is a Prime Minister of great learning vast administrative experience and impeccable 
reputation and also hon. Finance Minister, Shri P. Chindambaram, for waiving the agriculture 
loan to the extent of Rs. 60,000 crores for the benefit of millions of agriculturists in this vast 
sub-continent and also for the valuable measures ta ken by them for the benefit of the 
farmers in the country to enhance the agricultural production.  
When Tamil Nadu Government assumed Office in the year 2006, it immediately waived all 
the cooperative farm loans thereby rejuvenating the farming sector. Tamil Nadu Government 
also waived the cooperative crop loans to the tune of Rs. 7,000 crores in the State and then, 
it compensated the cooperative institutions providing Rs. 3,304 crores as financial assistance 
in a period of two years from 2006 to 2008, and further, a sum of Rs. 1,150 crores has been 
allocated for 2008-09 for the same purpose.  
We hope that the Union Government will provide financial assistance to the State towards 
cooperative farm loans waived by the Government of Tamil Nadu.  
The Tamil Nadu Government reduced the rate of inter est on crop loans given by the 
cooperative banks from nine to five per cent in the  recent Budget. Many agricultural 
economists have the opinion that interest rates of crop loans must be further reduced to 
four per cent. Accepting this recommendation, with a view to provide further fillip to 
agriculture, the rate of interest has been reduced to four per cent from this financial year.  
.

The Tamil Nadu Government will procure pulses from the farmers at the Minimum Support 
Price announced by the Union Government by providin g incentive of fifty rupees per 
quintal over and above the incentive price of hundred rupees per quintal announced by the 
Union Government, thereby enhancing the procurement  price of fine 'variety of paddy to 
Rs. 825/-per quintal.  
But based on the just demand that the procurement price of paddy should be at par with 
wheat and the recent recommendation of the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices, 
the Tamil Nadu Government will continue to urge the  Union Government to enhance the 
procurement price of paddy to Rs. 1000/- per quintal.  
The scheme for providing free power to all farmers which was introduced by the DMK 
Government in 1990 in Tamil Nadu still continues. A  subsidy of Rs. 268 crores has been 
provided in the Budget for 2008-09 to the Tamil Nadu Electricity Board for this scheme.

season, most of the States especially, Tamil Nadu s uffer water scarcity for agricultural 
development. A national program for interlinking of  our rivers in the country is the only 
solution, as advised by experts and our honorable M embers of the House, for sustaining 
and improving the agricultural production in the country. Because of the problems of inter-
State river water disputes and inadequate water supply, we face great hardships in agricultural 
development. In the absence of consensus among States, we urged that the Central assistance 
be provided, at least for the linking of inter-Stat e livers in Tamil Nadu as an emergency 
measure to save the crops.  
Accepting this request, the National Development Council has resolved to provide such 
assistance under the Accelerated Irrigation Assista nce Programme. In anticipation of this 
assistance, the following river linking projects in Tamil Nadu will be taken up in 2008-09 from 
the State-owned funds. The first phase of Cauvery-Agniar-Koraiyar-Pambar-Vaigai-Gondar 
interlinks scheme is for taking surplus flood water in Cauvery to water deficit Districts. The 
construction of Kattalai barrage across Cauvery wil be taken up at a cost of Rs. 165 crores.  
The next phase of work for excavating a 255-kilometer long canal linking these rivers will 
be taken up based on the detailed project report th at is under preparation. If each State has 
to depend on itself for agricultural development in  the absence of consensus amongst the 
State in sharing water, electricity, foodgrains or any other essential commodity, then, where 
is the possibility of national integration? We are talking very high of the nation's unity and 
responsibility of the States to cooperate with each  other by raising voices and shouting 
slogans which are nothing but emotions. If we are t o achieve the real meaning of national 
integration, we should be guided by the democratic principles outlined in the Constitution 
of India. I see friends coming from Kashmir to Kany akumari representing all the 28 States 
and 7 Union Territories in this august forum that h ave different culture, language and 
administration. We should respect each other's feel ings and necessities for the benefit of 
the people of this country. For that we should have a common principle which is "Unity in 
Diversity".  
With our unity, we should work hard to eradicate po verty and illiteracy among the 
farmers which are the major threats to the agricultural development of our nation. We have 
to be realistic in following the principles of national integration. We are the brothers of the 
same land, we are the sons of the soil. We should not have options according to our own  

Discussion on the working  [28 APRIL, 2008]     of the Ministry of Agriculture 267  
whims and fancies, but should compulsorily come for ward to the rescue of each other for 
agricultural growth and other welfare schemes. Only  then we can achieve the goal of 
independence and national integration thereby.  
Our country is mainly focussing its attention on developing information technology and 
other industries. Similarly, we should have increas ed focus towards research and 
development in the field of agriculture. We should allocate more funds for scientific research 
and development of agriculture through our benevole nt scientists like Prof. M.S. 
Swaminathan and others to enable the country to mar ch towards becoming an agricultural 
super power. Thank you.  
SHRI K.E. ISMAIL (Kerala)*: Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, our agrarian Sector is facing a 
severe crisis now. As a result food crisis also has developed into serious dimensions. If we 
allow the food crisis to grow beyond a limit, it wi ll explode into a food riot. This serious 
situation is the result of the wrong economic polic ies pursued by this Government. Our 
country is facing a tragic situation because of the  new economic policies adopted by the 
government. In the last 6 or 7 years we have discussed many times in this House how more 
than one and a half lakh farmers, neck-deep in debt and miseries, found the final solution in 
suicide. They had no alternative other than death w hen confronted with the harsh realities 
of life. But we failed to address these issues with  a sense of reality. This is in fact the 
biggest tragedy of our system.  
America and European countries give maximum assistance and subsidies to the farming 
sector in order to protect it. But pressurized by t hese very countries the Government of 
India is canceling the concessions and subsidies hi therto given to the agriculture sector. 
One of the main reasons of the present crisis is the removal of these subsidies.  
India is a country of tens of thousand of villages.  The progress of India is the progress 
of these villages. This is what Mahatma Gandhi said . More than seventy per cent of our 
population depend on agriculture for their lives. O ur country is an agrarian economy. The 
backbone of this country are the farmers of this co untry. It was with a view to achieve the 
development of our country through the development of peasant population that many 
schemes were implemented in the first three five year plans. So many changes took places 
in our country as a result of these schemes and the re was tremendous progress in the 
agriculture sector. But later, we retracted from that path and tempted by the new economic 
policies, we started neglecting the poor, the farme r, the village and the countryside. The 
present crisis is the result of this shift in the focus.  
So, I urge upon the government to take steps to imp lement comprehensive agrarian 
reforms. Centralization of land should be prevented. Land reforms as implemented in Kerala 
should be implemented throughout the country.  
Government should take action to help the farmer co mmunity by giving emphasis on 
production, increasing productivity, value added products, storing of agricultural products, 
ensuring fair prices for the producers, and ensurin g the welfare and security of farmers. 
Government should provide financial assistance for the overall development of agriculture 
and co-operative institutions should be strengthened to provide assistance to the farmers.  
Sir, Kerala is a deficit state as far as foodgrains are concerned. It is not a new development. 
It has been a deficit state for many years. Universal Public Distribution System was

established in Kerala as a result of the collective  demand of the people of the state during 
the period of the formation of single food region. Most of our agricultural products are cash 
crops. It was the initiative of the first Prime Min ister of the country.Pandit Jawahar Lai 
Nehru that the Universal Public Distribution System  was established in the state. The 
vision behind this was that a state, which produces cash crops and contributes considerably 
to the foreign exchange reserve of the country shou ld not face food shortage. There are 68 
lakh ration cardholders in the state today. Those p eople are in a deep crisis as they are not 
getting food grains. In such a situation the Honour able Minister, instead of providing 
sufficient quota of rice taking into consideration the special nature of the cash crop producing 
state, has decided to reduce the quota. The reason cited for the reduction in the quota is 
that the government which was in power in the state from 2001 to 2006 did not procure the 
full quota of rice. On the basis of this argument the Minister is punishing the people of the 
state now. Till now the quantum of rice supplied to the APL cardholders per month was one 
lakh thirteen thousand tons. Sir, this is now reduc ed to 17 thousand tons. The Honourable 
Minister should explain the reasons for this drasti c reduction. Sir, how is it possible to 
distribute rice among the people of the state with this meagre quota? Kerala is a state which 
gives ration to those below the poverty line and ev en to those above the poverty line 
defined by the Central Government.  
Sir, the food crisis has aggravated and the governm ent does not take any effective step. 
This food crisis is caused by the crisis in the agriculture sector. This crisis in the agriculture 
sector should be resolved. The Government should co me forward to spread an awareness 
among the people that farming is a profitable as we ll as a dignified profession. People 
should be encouraged to cultivate in the land avail able to them. So there should be a 
thorough change in the policies and approaches of t he Government. The Government 
should accept the principle that the development of  the country can be achieved through 
the development of agriculture. There should be com prehensive changes in the policies of 
the Government.  
VICE CHAIRMAN (SHRI TARIQ ANWAR): Thank you Mr. Ismail.  
SHRI K.E. ISMAIL: The present crisis can be overcome only by making thorough changes 
in the policies. I am not quoting any figures now because, Sir, you say that the time allotted 
to me is over. So, Sir, in order to prevent the cou ntry from being pushed' into a food riot 
action should be taken against hoarding and other m alpractices and steps should be taken 
to collect and store food grains. Sir, the practice  of renting out FCI godowns should be 
stopped. The Government should store food grains in  these godowns and supply them 
where they are needed and ensure that the farmers get good prices for their products. In this 
way the Government should take positive steps to im prove the situation in the agriculture 
sector. The Swaminathan Committee report is availab le. There are many long pending 
demands of the farmers of this country. These deman ds should be met on the basis of the 
recommendations in this report. We can not resolve the present crisis without addressing 
the serious issues related to farmers with a sense of reality. I urge upon the Government to 
take positive steps in that direction. With these words I conclude. Thank you.  
SHRI ABANI ROY (West Bengal): I must thank our colleague, Amar Singhji, for raising 
the discussion on the Ministry of Agriculture. Toda y, when we are discussing the matter, 
the officers of the Ministry of Agriculture are als o present there. The reason why I am 
raising this point is that Ministers come and Ministers go but officers remain there constantly. 
Yes, some transfers are there. Commission after Com mission submit their reports. If the  

Discussion on the working  [28 APRIL, 2008]     of the Ministry of Agriculture 269  
Department of the Ministry itself does not work pro perly, we will be unable to feed the 
people of India.  
I don't know. Seven reports have been submitted. If  they won't help the Minister, then it 
is a different thing because the Minister has to re ply to what is right and what is wrong. If 
there is any scarcity, it is the Minister who is re sponsible to give the answer. "But it is the 
Ministry, I think, who should properly guide the Mi nister what to do and what not to do, 
and in this particular case, on the question of 70 per cent of people who are in the villages 
and who are working, not only working, but also feeding you and all the people of India, and 
the farmers, who produce pulses and other things, a fter feeding the Indian people. They 
export these things to other countries from here. This normally happens. This had happened 
when the earth quake or any other natural calamity had taken place in the nearby countries, 
and we had to send rice, wheat and everthing to the m. So, it is my earnest request to the 
Ministry itself to decide whether we will have enou gh to feed the people of India. On the 
question of food security, I must say that the Department is well-equipped with technologists, 
with agricultural scientists and the uses of the ag ricultural universities. You know 
modernisation, and it is a shame that even after having a such a well-equipped Department, 
farmers have to commit suicides only due to the delay in the announcement of MSP, for not 
getting water for irrigation, only for not getting power, for not getting fertilizer. So, I request 
the Minister of Agriculture to convene a joint meet ing of various Ministries related with 
agriculture, that is, the Ministry of Agriculture, the Ministry of irrigation, the Ministry of 
Power, the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers and the Ministry of Finance of the Central 
Government as well as various Ministries of the Sta tes concerned with agriculture in order 
to ensure security of food, in order to run the PDS in a better way, in order to strengthen the 
PDS, and in order to procure the food grains, and I  think, for all this, a joint meeting and a 
joint decision is required, and I will urge upon th e Minister to convene such a meeting, not 
an-all party meeting, but a meeting of the State machinery as well as of the Central machinery 
to look into the matter so that we can give much mo re relief to the poor farmers. I am 
requesting the hon. Minister because he is such a M inister who is very much with the 
agriculture, and who is known as the king of agriculture in this State. So, you must think in 
this way. Whatever things you get from here, data is there, that can be utilised, and I will be 
glad if the report submitted by the hon.'Member, Dr . Swaminathan, who is sitting here, at 
least, the Minister can see to it that the report submitted by him, is implemented. With this, 
I thank you. I hope the hon. Minister will take not e of all this data and other things, and 
assure us that there will be no food crisis in India in future, and at this state, at least, he will 
do something as a Member of the UPA. He will do something for the aam admi what others 
are not doing or what others have not done. Thank you.

This is definitely reflected in procurement. What w as the procurement two years ago? 
This particular issue has been raised on a number o f occasions in the House. Now, our 
wheat procument was 91 lakh tonnes two years ago. This year we have finalised a target of

150 lakh tonnes. We started the procurement on Bais akhi, from the 14th of April, about 
10-11 days back. Generally, we complete this procurement in two-and-a-half to three months' 
time. The total market arrival was 133 lakh tonnes and out of 133 lakh tonnes, practically 
within ten days, the FCI could procure 126 lakh tonnes, that is, 94 per cent of the total arrival 
in the market. As compared to last year, it is more by 49.72 lakh tonnes. This is an achievement 
and I must give full credit to the farmers, specially, of Punjab and Haryana. Their contribution 
has been substantial. Whatever wheat arrival was th ere in the Punjab Mandis in the last 
eleven days, 99.2 per cent of that has been procure d and whatever wheat arrival was there 
in the Haryana Mandis, 99.9 per cent has been procured. I would like to give full compliments 
to Badal Saheb, the Chief Minister of Punjab and his entire machiney which has cooperated 
in this procurment and, similarly, Shri Bhupinder Singh Hooda and his entire cooperatives 
and other network which is helping day-and-night in procurement and in resolving country's 
food security problem.  
The same is true about rice. We have finalised a target of 270 lakh tonnes. The summer 
paddy has not yet come. It will start in another 15 days to one-month's time. But so far as the 
total procurement is concerned, up to the 27th of A pril, out of 270 lakh tonnes, we could 
procure 229 lakh tonnes and, if you compare it with  the last year, last year exactly on the 
same day we could procure 212 lakh tonnes. So, as c ompared to 212, we have done 229.1 
have to give full compliments to the Governments of  Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and 
Orissa. They have given tremendous support in the p rocess of this procurment of rice 
alongwith Punjab and Haryana. And I am confident that we will be able to achieve our entire 
target.  
In such a situation, definitely, hon. Members will ask a number of questions, like, if this 
is the overall position of wheat and rice, then why  this cut. Shri Vijayaraghavan and his 
colleages have raised on a number of occasions this particular subejct. And I can understand 
that. In Kerala, there is an altogether different s ituation as compared to other States. I am 
fully aware that Kerala is a State which produces p lantation crops which bring in a lot of 
money and which also earns a lot of foreign exchang e for the country. Essentially, the 
Kuttanad area produces substantial quantity of rice and this year was one of the exceptional 
years for paddy crop in that particular area. But we had unseasonal rains in that entire belt. 
And that has affected a substantial area of the pad dy crop in Kerala, in Tamil Nadu and in 
Andhra too. But, still, I think, we will, definitely, be able to - the respective State Governments 
are trying their level best to procure in all these  areas ~ get some good quantity from all 
these areas. Why have we taken these decision to re duce the APL quota? In fact, it is very 
interesting that we are discussing about the Agricu lture Ministry, but more discusison is 
taking place on the Food Ministry. Firstly, I would  like to clarify one thing. Shri Shanta 
Kumarji has raised one issue regarding the quantum of AAY and BPL. The quantum of AAY 
and BPL was fixed lastly as 35 kilogram per cardhol der per family. We have not changed 
that. Neither have we changed the prices. The prices which were fixed in the year 2002, are 
there even today. Even today, the Central Issue Price is the price which was fixed in 2002. 
We have not changed these prices, and there is no m odification. The subsidy burden has 
gone from Rs. 18,000 crores to somewhat near to 40,000 crores, 44,000 crores this year. It is 
because, in one way, we are improving the MSP and we are not changing the Central Issue 
Price for the Public Distribution System. It is tru e that we have not changed the AAY 
category; we have not changed the BPL category, but  we have taken a different approach 
about the APL category. What decision is taken by t he Government of India? We have 
appointed two committees. In fact, the previous Government had appointed one committee,  

274    Discussion on the working   [RAJYASABHA]  of the Ministry of Agriculture  
and one committee was appointed by the Planning Com mission just to study the Public 
Distribution System. And their report was really al arming. It is very difficult for me to disclose 
the names of the States, but in some of the States the diversion of the wheat was above 95 per 
cent. And in some of the states, the diversion of r ice and wheat both was between 30 per cent to 
55 per cent. We have carefully studied as to where the problem is. Out observation was, there 
was no problem in AAY category; there was very limited problem in BPL cateogy, but the real 
problem was in the APL category. Then, we have take n a decision that whatever quantity which 
has been allotted to each and every State continuously for three years for the APL and whatever 
quantum they have lifted in the last three years, we have made the average, and that average we 
have started to allot to all the States. It is beca use whatever they have lifted, we have started 
allotting, and that is why the problem arose. Suppo se, the allocation for a particular State was 
one lakh tonnes and their total n lifting was only 12,000 tonnes or 15,000, not only for one year, 
but also for one, two, three years, then there was no case to give more than 12,000 tonnes or 
13,000 tonnes. That is why a uniform decision was t aken to reduce the APL quantum. We have 
not reduced the AAY, and we have not reduced the BPL.  
Sir, it is true that now we started getting lot of enquiries and demands from various States and 
the basic reason is market prices. The prices of wh eat and rice two years back or the last year 
were somewhat near to our Central Issue Price of th e APL category. But, as the hon. Member, 
Shri Sharad Joshi has said, it is not only a domest ic problem of the country, but in the whole 
world the prices of foodgrains have become a serious issue. In fact, in my last discusison, I had 
briefed the Members of this august House about this  issue. But, just now I want to give one 
example here. One of the major countries which is producing and exporting rice is Thailand. In 
Indian currency, about six months back, the price of one kilogram rice of Thailand was somewhat 
near to Rs. 17 to Rs. 18. Today, the wholesale selling price is Rs. 40. This is not only in Thailand, 
but this is practically all over the world also, ou t of India. Similar is the situation about the 
prices of wheat; similar condition is about pulses, oilseeds and edible oil. Today, India is the only 
country where wheat and rice prices are the lowest as compared to any other country in the 
world.  
In such a situation, anybody can think, if this is the position, then why not restore the normal 
allocation because, there is more demand now? What happened to result in the sudden demand? 
One reason is the open market prices. The second re ason is, whatever economic growth we are 
observing is reflecting on the purchasing power. Th e third is, the National Rural Employment 
Gurantee Scheme, which is providing jobs to quite a  big number of people, and providing a 
substantial money, a few thousand crores, and out of that, our observation is, about 55 per cent of 
the wages go to buy the foodgrains and that is why there is more demand. % Though we have 
succeeded in producing much more in the last 30-40 years, still there is a mismatch between 
demand and supply and that is the reason why there is a pressure. But, I would like to assure all my 
colleagues from the Kerala State that we have taken some corrective decisions in the last week. I 
have to take a different approach about a few State s, especially Kerala and, probably, the 
Bundelkhand area of Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Prades h; the entire area is facing a serious 
drought and that is why we have to do something, we have to find some solution; we have to cut 
here and there and we have to protect the interests  of the affected people in these two States, 
especially the drought-pone area. I am sure, we wil l be able to take a decision in another week's 
time. Today, we have taken some corrective decision about Kerala but I am not sure whether I will 
be able to restore the entire quantum; but, definitely, we will see to it that the situation will ease  
in Kerala.  

Discussion on the working  [28 APRIL,. 2008]     of the Ministry of Agriculture 275  
Sir, there are a number of problems but, ultimately , we have to find some solution; we 
have to see how the farming community of this country will be able to resolve the country's 
problem and their own problems too. One of the major decisions which the Government of 
India has taken after assuming the power is the app ointment of the National Policy for 
Farmers and the National Commission for Fanners under the chairmanship of Dr. Swaminathan. 
We have received a few reports from him and we also  have received the final report. The 
major stake was to frame a pro-active policy, that is National Policy for Farmers, 2007. The 
policy included inter alia, asset reforms in respect of land, water, lifestyles , fisheries and 
bio-resources; support services and inputs like app lication on the fertile technologies for 
improving productivity in a sustainable manner; agr iculture-wise security system; supply 
of the good quality seeds and, disease-free planting material; issue of soil health pass-book 
for farmers and integrated nutrients; and fresh man agement system. The Department of 
Agricultural Cooperation has constituted an Inter-M inisterial Committee to prepare the 
plan of action for the operationalisation of the National Policy for Farmers. In fact, I will brief 
on some of the decisions which we have already taken, and the rest of the decisions, we are 
in the process of implementing. To address the ques tion of food security, the Central 
scheme has been recently announced; that is, the Na tional Food Security Mission, is 
launched in 311 identified districts and 17 States from the rabi, 2007, with an aim to achieve 
additional production of 20 million tonnes of the f oodgrains. This production will be 
essentially of wheat, rice and pulses. An issue was  raised that we have introduced the 
scheme but actually we have not provided enough fun ds. It is true that the total allocation 
for this entire scheme for five years is somewhat near to Rs.5000 crores. The allocation for 
the year 2007-08 is Rs. 397 crores. The.total amoun t released to 17 States and four public 
institutions during 2007-08 is Rs. 389 crores. It i s true that the amount is not enough. 
Suppose, if we have to send Rs. 5000 crores in five  years, it means we should provide Rs. 
1000 crores a year. But one should not forget that we started this scheme when the Rabi 
season started. So, we have missed the first kharif season. That is why the total requirement 
was somewhat near to it and that amount has been provided. And whatever the impediments 
we are seeing in the wheat and rice production, I t hink, this is one of the reasons. Those 
districts which have been selected for implementati on of this scheme, definitely, there is 
improvement and they have produced more. I am confi dent whatever the programme we 
would like to implement, I think, we will be able to achieve and this particular target, which 
has been decided, I think, we will be able to achieve. One of the Issues which was raised by 
hon. Shanta Kumarji and it is true that provision f or the agriculture and allied sector was 
going down but certain corrective decisions have de finitely been taken. I do not want to 
brief about or give more details about the previous regime, the NDA regime, but the maximum 
amount which was provided during the NDA regime was Rs. 10805 crores and prior to that it 
was some what near to Rs.8000 crores, Rs. 8200 cror es, Rs.8300 crores but from the year 
2004-05, from Rs.10000 crores it jumped to Rs.13000  crores, Rs. 15000 crores and Rs. 
18000 crores and plus these two schemes for the Foo d Security Mission, and second 
scheme, that is, one of the major schemes, RKVY has  been introduced. The real problem 
was that the State Governments were not providing sufficient fund for the agriculture. The 
hon. Prime Minister had to call a special meeting of the NDC on 29th May, 2007, and all the 
Chief Ministers were there and in that meeting it was decided to launch a new scheme, that 
is, Rashtriya Krisi Vikas Yojana, which was introduced in 2007 with an outlay of Rs.25000 
crores for the Eleventh Five Year Plan. Hon. Member , Viajayaraghavanji, has said that 
sufficient provision has not been made. It is corre ct but one should try to understand what 
is the scheme. The scheme is here and basically the  scheme is just to encourage States to 
provide money for agriculture. Whatever the budgetary provision which they have made

last year, over and above, if any State Government is ready to provide additional funds for 
agriculture or allied sector, the Government of Ind ia will contribute equivalent amount. So, 
our expectation was that all the States try to take advantage of this. But, this year, whatever 
proposals we got from various other States where th ey have provided additional funds to

getting from all the States, the States have taken this thing seriously, and I hope, from next 
year there will definitely be more provision for ag ricultural and allied sector in all State 
Budgets and whatever additional Budget provision wi ll be there that amount will be 
compensated from Government of India and I am confi dent that will definitely improve the 
overall position. There was a lot of discussion abo ut this waiver issue. One of the biggest

under this scheme. Our own assessment, the total responsibility will be Rs. 50,000 crores for 
total waiver to those who are below five acres and those who are above five acres, their one 
time settlement scheme, where 25 per cent will be w aived, we expect that about Rs. 10,000 
crores will be the burden. We have planned to provide money to the banks in three years in 
three instalments. Why these three years? In the ye ar 2004-05, when the Government came 
to power, in the first week or the first fifteen da ys we have announced a major decision and 
that is re-scheduling of all agricultural loans whi ch were outstanding and they have given 
five instalments and that is why still this re-sche dule amount period is not over that has to 
be repaid in five years time but still there are three years and in these three years ultimately, 
the farmer is supposed to pay this amount and that is why with the consultation of the 
banks, NABARD and Reserve Bank, ultimately these th ree instalment proposals were 
suggested and approved and enough provisions have a lready'been made. We raised two to 
three issues. In fact, one day in this august House  also, there Was a question about this
