Budgetary provision we would like to make is only for up to five acres. There are suggestions 
that those who are above five acres but come under the rain fed category, a different 
approach should be taken about them. It is true tha t we are also receiving a lot of 
recommendations and suggestions and there were shar p reactions also from some of the 
group of farmers who are regularly paying. Why are they penalised? Why not give some 
concessions to them? These issues are there. But, as on today, our thinking is, whatever the 
decision has been announced let us implement that a nd after implementation, one can think 
at least, those farmers who are rain fed and above 5 acres and those farmers who regularly 
repay, I think, they also deserve some sort of supp ort. I am confident we will be able to 
convince our Finance Ministry and all other concern ed departments and we will take 
appropriate decision at the appropriate time. One i ssue was raised about my home State by 
Mr. Vijayaraghavanji that this particular decision sought to benefit only a particular part of 
my State, i.e. Western Maharashtra. I am sorry, but that is not ac tually correct. In Western 
Maharashtra, the total number of farmers below five acres is 86 per cent. In Vidharbha, the 
total number of farmers is 63 per cent. Traditionally, in that area big lands were there, if you 
go to the entire coastal area, for instance, of Mah arashtra, about 95 per cent farm holdings 
are below one acre. That is why the number looks more. But, amount-wise, I think, benefits

were given to all regions. The decision is not taken for one State, but the decision is taken 
for the whole country.  
Sir, another important issue raised here is regardi ng the M.S.P. or remunerative prices. 
Shri Amar Singh has also raised this issue. He has said, 'Why are you not giving more 
money to wheat-grower of the country? Why are you i mporting? It is true. Whenever we 
have to take a decision to import; let me tell you frankly and to this august House, I will not 
get sleep on that night. Being a farmer, who always fought against import, it also pains me. 
But, certain decisions have to be taken where there is a question of food security. If our kitty 
is not full, we have no choice. We had imported twi ce. When we took the first decision on 
import, whatever amount that we had paid to outside rs was definitely less than the Central 
issue Price to domestic farmers. But, on our second and third purchases from outside India, 
we had paid more money. But, we had not brought any thing either from America or even 
from Australia. We had mostly bought from Russia, K azakhstan and Ukraine. Practically, 
there was no wheat available in other than these countries. Wheat was available in America. 
But, the Government of America was not ready to accept phytosanitary conditions of India. 
They were trying to pressurise us and requested us to modify these things. But, that was 
not in the interest of the Indian agriculture and I ndian farmers. That is why we took a 
conscious decision not to import from the USA. And, Australia itself was facing drought for 
the last two years. So, it had, practically, stopped any type of exports. So, whatever we had 
imported, we had imported from all these countries.  There might be some other countries 
also. But, definitely, it is not from the United States of America.  
Sir, we have taken a number of decisions on the M.S .P. In fact, the Government has 
substantially increased the M.S.P. for various comm odities. For instance, increase in the 
M.S.P for wheat and paddy in 2004-05 to 2007-08 was  Rs. 360 per quintal for wheat and 
Rs. 185 per quintal for paddy. In the previous regi me, the total increase was only Rs. 20 per 
quintal for wheat and Rs. 30 per quintal for paddy during 2001 -02 to 2004-05. In the previous 
regime, the total increase was only Rs. 20 and Rs. 30 that too in four or five years. Against 
that, we have given Rs. 185 and Rs. 360. In fact, this is one of the reasons that since enough 
remunerative prices was not given and that is why s uddenly farmers started reducing the 
area of cultivation for wheat and paddy and this ha s affected the country's production. We 
have taken the corrective measures. I know that the re is a demand that we should increase 
the price. But this also reflects, ultimately, in t he open market prices. When we have given 
Rs. 1,000 per quintal to wheat, there is 12.5 per c ent local Government charges for every 
Rs. 1,000 plus other expenses and, ultimately, the cost goes up to Rs. 1,400 per quintal. If the 
cost goes to Rs. 1,400, automatically, the domestic  prices, in the open market, also goes 
above and that ultimately lead to rise in prices of essential commodities. Similarly, there is a 
request that we should take a decision of giving Rs. 1,000 for paddy. If you give Rs. 1000 for 
paddy, the Government or the FCI will get only 60 kg. rice. We do not get 100 kgs rice. That 
means, Rs. 1,000 will be the price for 60 kgs. of r ice. Ultimately, the selling price will be 
somewhat Rs. 16 -17 per kilogram. Automatically, the market prices will go up. And, there will 
definitely be a serious problem of rising prices. I n such a situation, we have to see that we 
should provide better remunerative price for the fa rmers. It should be cost-effective. He 
should not be disheartened. He should get a good re turn. Simultaneously, we have to 
protect the interests of the consumer also because farmer himself is also a consumer. He is 
not producing each and every item. I am a farmer, I don't produce rice. I buy rice from open * 
market. Similar is the situation of the farmers from different parts of the country also. That's 
why we have to take a sort of a balanced approach a bout the remunerative prices.

There was a lot of discussion about the rain-fed area and drought. The Government took 
a major decision to appoint a National Rainfed Area Authority in 2007. The Authority is not 
supposed to provide money and to start work. It is supposed to issue guidance and technical 
support to various States and coordinate among various agencies. So, we have started the 
work of this authority. I am sure that we will pay enough attention to the rainfed agricultural. 
And, the sixty per cent of the entire agriculture production is from 40 irrigated area, and rest 
of the 40 per cent production is from the rainfed areas. That's why if we have to overall 
improve the agricultural production, we cannot neglect the rainfed areas. That's the reason 
the same had particularly been allowed by the Prime Minister on 15th August. We have 
practically started implementing that.  
Hon. Member, Shri Shanta Kumar, had raised the issue of Extension Services. In Mat 
2005, reforms in Extension Services had been launched by the Agricultural Ministry. An 
autonomous body by the name of the Agriculture Technological Management Agency 
(ATMA) at the district level with an active participation of the farmers, farmer groups, 
NGOs, Krishi Vigyan Kendras, panchayat raj institutions, and other stakeholders. It operates 
at district level and below. It has been implemented in 470 districts of 27 States and two 
Union Territories till today. So, this is one of the major decisions that has been taken. I am 
sure this decision will really be helpful. Whatever research has been developed by the 
ICAR and their various research institutes, our effort is to see that their research reaches 
from lab to land. This particular organization is taking this entire responsibility about this 
implementation.  
Another issue was raised here about the marketing. Hon. Sharad Joshi has said that 
there should not be any restriction. The farmer should be allowed to sell their produce. It is 
his basic right to get a proper price. One of the organizations was definitely coming in the 
way, that is, the Agriculture Produce Market Committee and their Act. Under the APMC Act, 
there was a restriction on the farmer that he is supposed to sell his produce only in regulated 
market and only to a licensee trader. A decision was taken, in fact, six years back, prior to this 
Government that we should amend these rules. And, this decision was not taken just by the 
Government, a meeting of the Chiet Ministers was called by the former Prime Minister, Shri 
Atal Bihar Vajpayee.- In that meeting, this issue was discussed and, ultimately, a decision 
was taken. We feel that that was a correct decision. And, we have decided to implement that. 
Today, eighteen State Governments have taken the corrective action about the amendment 
in the APMC. And, there are seven States that do not have any APMC Act. So, as on today,* 
in most of the States, farmer has got every right to sell his produce anywhere and to 
anybody. One of the important problems which we are facing in various States is that the* 
is no proper infrastructure of the market where the farmer can take his produce and sell. The 
Government of India has taken a decision to establish terminal markets, duly linked to the 
farmers. These will be set-up in public-private participation mode. They will provide a 
quality market infrastructure, and will be directly linked to the farmer. States have called for 
Expression of Interest. About 20 locations have been selected by most of the Sates. I hope 
they will be able to take all the decisions, and proper work will be started within no time. 
Some of the States will be able to set-up these terminal markets which will be, ultimately, 
beneficial to the farmers.  
In the last 2-3 years, on many occasions, the issue of farmers' suicides has been discussed 
in this House and, practically, throughout India. We have taken certain collective decisions. 
There is improvement; but, still the situation is not that satisfactory. Dr. Jalan has raised this"  

Discussion on the working  [28 APRIL, 2008]     of the Ministry of Agriculture 279  
issue. Dr. Swaminathan has given some suggestions. It was also suggested that we should 
discuss this issue for the whole day. We should sit  together, try to find some solution, try 
to understand the gravity of the situation, and, if it is possible we should take more collective 
decisions. There is no hesitation from our side. We will be quite unhappy because whatever 
is happening is, definitely, not good for the count ry and, it is, definitely, not good for the 
farming community as a whole. But, we have taken some decisions, which I have briefed to 
the House on some other occasions also.  
The Government of India has approved a rehabilitation package of Rs. 16,978 crores to 
' 31 suicide-prone districts of the States, that is, in Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka 
and Kerala. And, they are supposed to implement thi s decision in three-years' time. The 
^formation regarding the number of suicides committ ed by the farmers during the year 
2007-08 in Vidharbha region has been communicated t o us by the Government of 
Maharashtra. So, we are going by their information.  The latest information which has been 
communicated to us is this. During the year 2007, t he figure of suicides committed by the 
farmers in Vidharbha region of Maharashtra was 1230 . Last year, it was 1448. In Andhra 
Pradesh, during 2007, up to September 2007, the number of suicides committed by farmers 
was 142. And, last year, exactly during the same period, it was 514. So, the number has come 
down. The Karnataka Government has communicated tha t during the year 2007-08, the 
number Up to July 2007 was 73 as compared to the figure of 320 last year of the same period. 
The Government of Kerala has communicated that the number of suicides committed by 
farmers in the first ten months in 2007, that is, up to October 2007 was 64 as compared to 841 
during the period 2001-2006, where the yearly avera ge was 140 suicides per year. So, in 
Kerala also, the number has come down substantially . Definitely, some improvement is 
there. I don't say that the situation has totally i mproved. We have to take a lot of corrective 
measures. We have to take the State Governments int o confidence. If there are some other 
issues also, we have to see how we will be able to solve them. We can accept any other 
thing, but these continuous suicides in the farming  community and by farmers in certain 
areas, is not good for any country.  
I do not want to say more about agricultural credit because previously we had given all 
the figures about what exactly we are doing.  
One of the issues raised here was that we have appointed many committees, we have not 
taken proper decisions, and that all these reports are still pending with the Government. In 
fact, that is not the factual position. A task force under the Chairmanship of Prof. Vaidyanathan 
to suggest measures for revival of Cooperative Credit Institutions was appointed. We have 
^ceived their report also. There is a recommendatio n for providing financial package of 
Rs. 14,839 crore for short-term rural credit institutions. The Government of India has approved 
this package for the revival of the short-term rura l cooperative credit sector involving 
financial assistance of Rs. 13,596 crores. The Stat e Governments have started taking 
corrective actions. They are supposed to complete t he audit of all these societies and the 
money will be released. Some of the States have alr eady received money biirall the States 
have not completed their entire work yet.  
Sir, one issue was raised about the milk production. In fact, in the whole world, there is a 
shortage of milk, but, in our country, the situation is little different. We have the shortage of 
milk only in two States, i.e., Kerala and West Bengal. In Karnataka, there is surplus milk; in 
Gujarat, there is surplus milk; in Maharashtra, there is surplus milk. Both Governments have 
taken corrective actions. They have got substantial quantity of milk powder and they are  

280   Discussion on the working   [RAJYASABHA]  of the Ministry of Agriculture  
trying to resolve their own problem. But here whether it is poultry, whether it is dairy or whether it is 
fishery, a number of decisions have been taken by the Government of India to help this particular 
section. It is true that the fisherman of this country belongs to one of the weakest sections of the 
society. Lot of women are also involved in this particular trade. The National Fisheries Board has 
been set up in the year 2007 in the area of 'Fish Capture Culture—Processing and Marketing' with 
modern tools of research and development, and our effort is that we should get 6-7 per cent growth 
in sub-sectors in the Eleventh Plan period and enough fund has been provided for this purpose. 
The headquarters has been set up in Hyderabad and the work has already been started.  
The irrigation issue was also raised here. In fact, this year, more provision has been made for the 
Accelerated Irrigation Benefit Programme, and number of other decisions are also taken by this 
Government. One of important issues, which was also discussed at the time of General Budget and 
Budget announcement also, is that soil condition of the land is a serious problem and that is why 
Dr. Swaminathan Committee had also recommended that we should take corrective decision. 
Therefore, we have taken decision to take up soil t esting mobile laboratories and other 
laboratories. In fact, it was announced in this year's Budget that 505 testing laboratories will be set 
up both in the public and private sectors during the Eleventh Plan period with a Government's assistance 
of Rs. 30 lakhs per laboratory. In addition, one fully-fitted mobile soil-testing laboratory will be provided 
to 250 districts of the country before March, 2009. So, we are in the implementation stage of this 
particular scheme.  
Regarding Krishi Vigyan Kendra, certain points have been suggested. I am ready to accept one 
suggestion which has been made by an hon. Member. Our today's decision is to give one Krishi 
Vigyan Kendra to every district, but there are some districts where the total area is much more like 
Jaisalmer, etc. There are certain decisions. So, one Krishi Vigyan Kendra is not sufficient. We have 
studied this particular subject and we have come to the conclusion that at least there are fifty districts 
as such where there has to be more than one Krishi Vigyan Kendra and we are going to set up these 
Krishi Vigyan Kendras in all these areas. 
I need not take time of this august House in narrating the contribution of the Indian Agriculture 
Research Institute. They have done a number of things. 'Quality seed production in the agricultural crops 
and fishery' was also launched. There are 37 agricultural universities and 47 agricultural institutes. They 
have taken the responsibility for seed production in the field of crop, horticulture crop and fishery. 
They have also developed a number of varieties of seeds, especially certain types of seeds which 
would enhance productivity and production. Three hundred and fifty varieties and hybrids of 
different crops including horticultural crops and vegetables were released and identified for 
cultivation in different parts of the country during the last four years. So, lot of work has been done 
there.  
An issue was raised by hon. Member, Shri Amar Singh, regarding genetically modified seeds. 
There is only one crop which has been approved thus and that is cotton. A series of trials took place 
in the last seven to eight years and, ultimately, our Approval Committee gave approval for the 
production of Bt Cotton in this country. There are different types and varieties which have been 
developed by our own Cotton Research Institute. It is true that there are certain genes which have 
been taken from foreign companies, but our own ICR Institute have also developed new varieties and 
whatever is available today in the country has been thoroughly tested and there is a good demand 
from the farming community. But  

Discussion on the working  [28 APRIL, 2008]     of the Ministry of Agriculture 281  
we have not selected, we have not developed a singl e such seed; research is going on, but 
neither in the area of food grains nor vegetables, any variety has been released which has 
been genetically modified. As hon. Member, Dr. Swaminathan has said, I entirely agree with 
him, that one can take full advantage of it and use  it for the benefit of the society also, but 
it can cause harm also. So, our effort, Sir, is, to  keep away whatever can cause harm; don't 
encourage; don't follow blindly the GM varieties; take full precautions; carry out a number 
of experiments in different seasons, in different p arts of the country for years together, not 
only in one or two years, six or seven years and, t hen, ultimately, take a final view. So, we 
have not taken any final view about all these things.  
Lastly, one important issue has been raised here ab out climate change. A High Power 
Committee has been appointed under the Chairmanship  of the hon. Prime Minister, with 
Scientists, experts and others associated with it. We are also separately working on what 
would be the impact of the climate change on Indian agriculture and we have geared up the 
Indian Council for Agricultural Research and all th e other institutions to concentrate in 
those areas and develop such varieties which would be resistant to high heat and which 
would not reduce any production. This is a continuo us process. It might take two-three 
years, but we are in touch; we are also keeping clo se touch with different countries. Also, 
we have no hesitation in trying and getting more in formation about whatever is available 
even outside India in this area and our efforts wou ld be to protect Indian agriculture from 
the effects of climate change. This year, the predi ction that we have got about monsoons 
are quite encouraging and we hope that this year al so we would enjoy one of the best 
seasons. And for that we have prepared from all ang les, whether it is inputs like fertilizers, 
pesticides, seeds or agricultural credit, and I am confident that in such a situation, the 
Indian farmers would come forward to help solve the country's problems. (Ends)  
SHRI ARJUN KUMAR SENGUPTA(West Bengal): Sir, if you permit me, I would like to 
raise only one issue, particularly because this is a very good year and the Members has 
given us very good news; this is about Public Distr ibution System, Sir, Public Distribution 
System in a globalising economy has a different rol e to play than simple radon shops. That 
is because, in a globalising economy, the demand is expanding either because of smuggling, 
because of cost-push or because of the level of increase in income. So, if there is an increase 
in supply, there will be some reduction in the pressure on price but the prices will not come 
down. And that is why the Public Distribution Syste m was invented, mainly to protect the 
poorest sections. And that can be done only by issu ing to them food grains at a cheaper 
price than the market price. That is the rationale behind the Public Distribution System and 
that is why we have the BPL categories. But the APL  category also belongs to the same 
group, even if they may not be equivalent to the BP L, they are only slightly better off and 
they are also equally affected. Just because there is a possibility of leakage in the normal 
years, in a particularly difficult year when the pr ices are going up—there is a globalising 
economy, whole world prices are going up—you must p rotect a large number of poor 
people, whether they are BPL or APL, by increasing the supply of the PDS system. Sir, 
today, you have got the opportunity because your pr oduction has increased and your 
procurement has increased. I hope, Sir, you will pr ovide that leadership of giving a new 
shape or new interpretation to the Public Distritbi on System and meet the demands of both 
the BPL and APL.
